paragraphs: Among aristocratic nations all the members of the community are connected with one another and depend on one another. The graduated scale of ranks acts as a tie that keeps everyone in his proper place and the whole body in subordination. Something of the same kind always happens in the political assemblies of these nations. Parties naturally group themselves under certain leaders, whom they obey by a kind of instinct that is only the result of habits formed elsewhere. They carry the habits and customs of general society into the smaller gathering.

In democratic countries it often happens that a great number of citizens are heading toward the same point, but each one moves there of his own accord, or at least flatters himself that he does. He is used to governing his actions by personal impulse alone, and he does not willingly submit to dictation from outside. This taste and habit of independence goes with him into the councils of the nation. If he agrees to join with other men in pursuing the same purpose, he still insists on remaining free to contribute to the common success in his own way. This is why, in democratic countries, parties are so impatient of control and can be managed only in moments of great public danger. Even then, the authority of leaders may be able to make men act or speak, but it hardly ever reaches the point of making them keep silent.

In aristocratic nations, the men who sit in political assemblies also belong to the aristocracy. Each has a high, settled rank of his own, and his seat in the assembly often matters less to him than his standing in the country. That standing comforts him when he takes no part in debates on public affairs, and it stops him from eagerly seeking a trivial one.

In America, it generally happens that a Representative becomes somebody only through his position in the Assembly. He is therefore constantly haunted by a craving to gain importance there, and he feels a restless desire to keep pushing his opinions on the House. His own vanity is not the only thing urging him along this course; so are his constituents, and so is the constant need to win their favor. Among aristocratic nations a member of the legislature is rarely strictly dependent on his constituents. He is often, to them, a kind of unavoidable representative; sometimes they are themselves strictly dependent on him. If they finally reject him, he can easily get elected elsewhere, or, retiring from public life, he can still enjoy the pleasures of a splendid idleness. In a democratic country like the United States, a Representative hardly ever has a lasting hold on the minds of his constituents. However small an electoral body may be, the shifting currents of democracy are constantly changing its character, so it must be courted without end. He is never sure of his supporters, and if they abandon him he is left without any resource. His natural position is not high enough for him to be easily known to people who are not close to him, and, given the complete independence prevailing among the people, he cannot hope that his friends or the government will send him down to be returned by an electoral body that does not know him. The seeds of his fortune are therefore sown in his own neighborhood. From that corner of the earth he must start, to raise himself to the command of a people and to influence the destinies of the world. So it is natural that in democratic countries the members of political assemblies think more of their constituents than of their party, whereas in aristocracies they think more of their party than of their constituents.

But what ought to be said to please constituents is not always what ought to be said to serve the party to which Representatives profess to belong. The general interest of a party often requires that its members not speak on great questions they understand imperfectly. It requires that they speak little on those minor questions that get in the way of the great ones. Finally, and in most cases, it requires that they not speak at all. Keeping silent is the most useful service a mediocre speaker can render to the commonwealth. Constituents, however, do not think so. The people of a district send a representative to take part in the government of the country because they hold a very high opinion of his merits. Men appear greater in proportion to the smallness of the things around them, so we may assume that the opinion held of the delegate will be higher the rarer talents are among his constituents. It will therefore often happen that the less his constituents have to expect from their representative, the more they will expect from him. However unfit he may be, they will not fail to call on him for remarkable efforts that match the rank they have given him.

Apart from his position as a legislator of the State, electors also regard their Representative as the natural patron of the constituency in the legislature. They almost consider him the proxy of each of his supporters, and they flatter themselves that he will be no less zealous in defending their private interests than those of the country. Electors are therefore quite sure in advance that the Representative of their choice will be an orator. They expect him to speak often if he can. If he is forced to hold back, they expect him at least to squeeze into his rarer speeches a review of all the great questions of state, together with an account of all the petty grievances they themselves have to complain of. Even if he cannot come forward often, he should prove what he is capable of on each occasion. Instead of constantly lavishing his powers, he should now and then condense them into a small space, so as to give a complete and brilliant summary of his constituents and of himself. On these terms they will vote for him at the next election. These conditions drive worthy men of modest abilities to despair; knowing their own powers, they would never have come forward voluntarily. But pushed on in this way, the Representative begins to speak, to the great alarm of his friends. Rushing recklessly into the midst of the most celebrated orators, he muddles the debate and wearies the House.

All laws that tend to make the Representative more dependent on the elector affect not only the conduct of legislators, as I have remarked elsewhere, but also their language. They influence at once the business itself and the manner in which the business is discussed.

There is hardly a member of Congress who can bring himself to go home without having sent at least one speech to his constituents. None of them will put up with any interruption until he has worked into his harangue whatever useful suggestions may be made about the four-and-twenty States of which the Union is composed, and especially about the district he represents. He therefore presents his listeners with a succession of great general truths, which he himself understands and expresses only confusedly, and of petty details, which he is only too able to discover and point out. The result is that the debates of that great assembly are often vague and confused, and seem to drag their slow length along rather than advance toward a clear object. Some such state of things will, I believe, always arise in the public assemblies of democracies.

Favorable circumstances and good laws might succeed in drawing to the legislature of a democratic people men far superior to those the Americans send to Congress. But nothing will ever prevent the men of slender abilities who sit there from pushing themselves complacently, and in every way, on the public. The evil does not seem to me capable of a complete cure, because it originates not only in the procedures of that assembly but in its constitution and in that of the country. The inhabitants of the United States themselves seem to see the matter this way. They show their long experience of parliamentary life not by refraining from making bad speeches but by courageously submitting to hear them. They are resigned to it, as to an evil they know to be unavoidable.

We have shown the petty side of political debates in democratic assemblies; let us now show the more imposing side. The proceedings of the Parliament of England for the last one hundred and fifty years have never caused any great stir outside that country. The opinions and feelings expressed by the speakers have never awakened much sympathy, even among the nations placed nearest to the great arena of British liberty. Europe, by contrast, was excited by the very first debates held in the small colonial assemblies of America at the time of the Revolution. This was due not only to particular and accidental circumstances but to general and lasting causes. I can imagine nothing more admirable or more powerful than a great orator debating great questions of state in a democratic assembly. No particular class is ever represented there by men commissioned to defend its own interests, so the orator always speaks to the whole nation and in the name of the whole nation. This enlarges his thoughts and heightens his power of language. Precedents have little weight there. No privileges are attached to certain property any longer, and no rights belong to certain bodies or certain individuals. The mind must therefore turn to general truths drawn from human nature to settle the particular question under discussion. Hence the political debates of a democratic people, however small it may be, have a breadth that often makes them attractive to mankind. All men are interested in them, because they deal with man, who is the same everywhere. Among the greatest aristocratic nations, on the contrary, the most general questions are almost always argued on some special grounds drawn from the practice of a particular time or the rights of a particular class. These interest only that class, or at most the people among whom that class happens to exist. This, as much as the greatness of the French people and the favorable disposition of the nations who listen to them, explains the great effect that French political debates sometimes produce in the world. The orators of France often speak to mankind, even when they are addressing only their countrymen.
